title: IB Maths AA Past Papers: A Final-Weeks Revision Plan
summary: Use IB Maths AA past papers to turn timed attempts into marks with careful self-marking, an error log and focused practice in the final weeks before exams.
body_markdown:
The most useful way to revise with IB Maths AA exam papers in the final weeks is to repeat a simple cycle: attempt under timed conditions, mark carefully, record why marks were lost, repair the weakest method, then test it again. Completing a paper gives you information. Acting on that information is what can improve your next performance.


Imagine a student finishing a difficult paper and immediately reaching for another. The impulse is understandable. Another attempt feels productive. But if the same algebra mistake survives into tomorrow, the extra work has left an important problem untouched.


The final weeks reward a more deliberate approach. Here is how to turn each attempt into a useful revision decision.


### Your final-weeks checklist


Before starting, prepare:


- An unseen AA paper that matches your level and assessment session.
- Its matching markscheme, kept closed until you finish.
- The permitted formula booklet and equipment.
- A timer and a short error log.
- Time afterwards for marking and targeted practice.


Check the duration and calculator instructions on the paper itself. Online advice can mix assessment versions, so your teacher’s guidance and the instructions for your examination session should determine your practice conditions.


### Start with a timed attempt that tells the truth


Your first full attempt should establish what happens when you work independently. Put away worked solutions, messages and revision notes. Use the calculator only where permitted, and stop when the allocated time ends.


A score becomes useful when you can trust the conditions behind it. Pausing the clock to look up a technique hides the exact difficulty you need to address.


During the attempt, mark questions you want to revisit. If you become stuck, write a plausible first step, leave space and move on. Return when you have collected the marks you can access elsewhere. RevisionDojo’s guide to[managing time in IB Maths exams](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-master-time-management-in-ib-math-exams) can help you build a pacing routine.


After time expires, draw a line beneath your work. You may continue briefly in a different colour to investigate unfinished questions. Keep those additions separate from your timed score: they help distinguish a time problem from a knowledge problem.


### Use the IB Maths AA markscheme as feedback


Self-marking requires more care than comparing final answers. Read the marking instructions and follow how credit is allocated throughout the solution.


Ask three questions for each lost mark:


- Did I choose a valid method?
- Did I carry it out accurately?
- Did I communicate the required result or justification?


Award credit for what is visible on your page. A method you intended to use cannot provide reliable evidence of what you could reproduce in an exam. Equally, do not assume an incorrect final answer means every earlier step earns zero. Apply the actual scheme, including any stated rules about errors carried forward.


Suppose you differentiate correctly but solve the resulting equation incorrectly. Your repair task is more specific than “revise calculus”: you need to practise the algebra that follows differentiation.


If your valid approach differs from the published solution and the credit is unclear, flag it for your teacher. RevisionDojo’s Grading tools can provide another source of feedback, but use the matching markscheme and teacher guidance to resolve uncertain awards.


### Keep an error log you will actually revisit


A useful error log is short enough to review before the next attempt. Record the question reference, the cause of the error and a concrete action.


Error observed Likely cause Next action


Lost a negative sign when expanding Algebra accuracy Practise several expansions and check each sign


Found stationary points but gave no classification Incomplete method Rehearse a valid classification test


Calculator returned an unexpected trig value Incorrect angle setting Check the required angle mode before solving


Left a long question unfinished Pacing or delayed method choice Retry a similar question under a time limit


Avoid entries such as “careless” or “bad at functions”. Neither tells you what to do tomorrow. “Forgot the domain restriction when finding an inverse” gives you a repair task.


Look for patterns across attempts. RevisionDojo’s guide to[common IB Maths AA mistakes](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-maths-aa-most-common-mistakes) offers another way to identify recurring weaknesses. Prioritise errors that appear repeatedly and affect methods used across several topics.


A student questions a calculator under a desk lamp about a missing minus sign, and the calculator asks to see the working.


### Turn weak topics into focused IB Maths AA practice


Once you identify a weakness, step away from full papers long enough to repair it.


Start by attempting the failed question again without reading the solution. If you cannot progress, review the relevant explanation, close it, and reconstruct the method independently. Then solve unfamiliar questions that require the same skill.


For example, a difficulty with logarithmic equations might lead to a short review of logarithm laws, followed by questions involving different bases and domain restrictions. The unfamiliar examples show whether you understand the method beyond one remembered solution.


Use[RevisionDojo’s Maths AA Questionbank](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-math-aa/questionbank) for this targeted practice. Study Notes can help rebuild an explanation; Flashcards can support recall of conditions and identities. When a particular step remains unclear, use AI Chat to ask why it is valid, then check the explanation against your course materials.


Revisit the skill after a gap, mixed with other topics. Solving it immediately after reviewing the answer is encouraging. Solving it independently later provides stronger evidence that the repair has lasted.


### Give the remaining weeks different jobs


A practical plan changes as the exam approaches. Adjust this outline around your other subjects and the time you have available.


### Earlier in the final weeks


Complete a timed diagnostic attempt, then spend the following sessions addressing its most important weaknesses. Preserve some unseen material for later checks. The[Maths AA SL revision guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-revise-ib-maths-aa-sl) provides further structure for SL students.


### During the final full week


Alternate timed work with correction sessions. Include practice for each component you will sit, following its calculator rules. HL students should also rehearse sustained reasoning across linked questions.


Use Mock Exams or Predicted Papers as additional practice where appropriate. Treat them as opportunities to test your preparation; they cannot guarantee which questions will appear.


### During the final days


Review recurring errors, practise a manageable mixed set and check calculator routines. Avoid beginning a demanding full paper so late that you cannot review it properly. RevisionDojo’s[last-minute Maths AA priorities](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-maths-aa-last-minute-revision-priorities) can help you narrow the remaining work.


### Make the next attempt show what changed


Before each new timed attempt, choose one behaviour to improve: show substitutions clearly, check domains, or move on sooner when stuck. Afterwards, check whether that behaviour changed and whether the targeted error returned.


RevisionDojo brings the revision cycle together, from Questionbank practice and Study Notes to feedback and timed assessment. Tutors can help resolve a persistent obstacle; the Coursework Library serves a separate purpose when you need coursework guidance.


Start with the weakest method in your error log. Practise it in the Questionbank, then sit timed papers in Exam mode to test whether the improvement holds under pressure. Each reviewed attempt should leave you with a clearer decision about what to practise next.
